mcqs.question: For a continuous random variable, what is P(X = 5) exactly?
options: Equal to the PDF value f(5)
Always exactly 0, since a single point has zero width under the density curve
Always exactly 1
It depends on the CDF at 5
mcqs.explanation: For continuous distributions, probability corresponds to area under the PDF over an interval — a single point has zero width, hence zero area, hence P(X=5)=0 regardless of how large f(5) is. Only ranges have nonzero probability.

mcqs.question: You flip a fair coin 10 times and want the probability of exactly 6 heads. Which distribution applies?
options: Poisson, since it involves counting
Exponential, since it involves flips over time
Binomial, since it's a fixed number of independent identical trials with two outcomes
Normal, since coin flips are common
mcqs.explanation: A fixed number of independent, identically-distributed two-outcome trials (10 flips, each with the same P(heads)) is the textbook definition of Binomial — Poisson applies to unbounded rare-event counts, not fixed trial counts.

mcqs.question: Why is Poisson described as a limiting case of Binomial?
options: They are unrelated distributions that happen to share notation
Binomial is always more accurate than Poisson
Poisson only applies when p = 0.5
As n grows large and p shrinks toward 0 while np stays fixed at λ, Binomial's shape converges to Poisson's
mcqs.explanation: Splitting a fixed interval into ever-finer sub-intervals (n→∞) each with vanishingly small event probability (p→0) while keeping the expected count np=λ fixed is exactly the derivation connecting Binomial to Poisson.

mcqs.question: Why do averaged metrics (like average response time across many requests) tend to look approximately Normal, even if individual response times don't?
options: The Central Limit Theorem: sums/averages of many independent random variables converge toward a Normal distribution regardless of the individual variables' own distribution
Coincidence — there's no theoretical reason
Because response times are always Normal to begin with
Normal distribution is required by definition for any average
mcqs.explanation: The Central Limit Theorem is precisely the guarantee that averaging many independent contributions smooths out toward Normal, no matter what the individual underlying distribution looks like — this is why Normal shows up so pervasively in aggregated real-world data.

mcqs.question: You've waited 10 minutes for a bus whose arrival follows an exponential distribution. What does memorylessness say about your expected remaining wait?
options: It's now shorter than the original expected wait, since you've already waited a while
It's exactly the same as if you'd just started waiting, unaffected by the 10 minutes already elapsed
It's now longer, since buses are 'due' to keep being late
Memorylessness doesn't apply to wait times, only counts
mcqs.explanation: Memorylessness is the defining, counter-intuitive property of the exponential distribution: the remaining wait time's distribution is identical regardless of how long you've already waited — the 10 elapsed minutes carry no predictive information.

mcqs.question: You want to model the number of customer support tickets arriving per hour, where tickets are rare and independent. Which distribution fits best?
options: Binomial, since you're counting
Uniform, since tickets could arrive at any time
Poisson, since it's an unbounded count of rare independent events in a fixed time interval
Exponential, since you're counting tickets, not measuring time
mcqs.explanation: Poisson is specifically designed for counting rare, independent events over a fixed interval with a known average rate — Binomial would need a fixed, known number of 'trials,' which doesn't naturally apply to an open-ended arrival count.

mcqs.question: A service averaging λ=2 errors/hour sees 12 errors in one hour. Why is this a stronger signal to investigate than seeing 5 errors?
options: It isn't stronger — any deviation from λ=2 is equally suspicious regardless of size
Because 12 is an even number and 5 is odd, which changes the Poisson formula's behavior
Because the Poisson model treats all outcomes above the mean as equally likely

Because P(X=12) under a λ=2 Poisson model is vastly smaller than P(X=5) — it's far more outcomes' worth of deviation from what the normal-rate model predicts, making it much stronger evidence that the rate itself has changed
mcqs.explanation: Poisson probabilities drop off sharply as the count moves further from λ — P(X=12) under λ=2 is dramatically smaller than P(X=5), so observing 12 is far stronger evidence against 'this is just normal variance around λ=2' than observing 5 is. Parity (even/odd) has no bearing on the calculation, and outcomes are not equally likely under Poisson — they're weighted by how far they sit from the mean.
